strengths: The paper addresses an important auditing problem: determining what can be inferred about an existing classifier when only aggregate label statistics are available. The formulation is relevant to proprietary classifiers and settings without representative individual-level validation data.

The shared-baseline mixture model provides a precise interpretation of the proposed unfairness measure. Its bounded range and monotonicity under merging prediction categories are useful properties, and the framework accommodates multiple classes and protected groups.

The finite-candidate characterization for binary unfairness and the reduction of binary discrepancy optimization to one-dimensional searches are valuable technical ideas. Experiments cover hundreds of binary classification tasks and several multiclass applications; the initialization ablations demonstrate improvements, and some known-confusion-matrix bounds coincide.
Detailed derivations, pseudocode, an appendix proof, and a public code link support informed examination and reproduction.
weaknesses: The discrepancy guarantees require mathematical correction. Section 7.1 applies τβ(a,b)=βη(a,b)+(1−β)(1−b) to false-positive/false-negative rates, reversing the intended error term. Equations (26) and (29) omit the population/class weights from their error term. More substantively, Lemma 7.3 bounds the derivative of η but neglects τβ's additional linear term: with β=0.5 and (a,b,c,d)=(0.2,0.4,0.1,0.2), its bound is zero although |ψ′|=0.1. These issues require reconciling the derivations with the implementation and revalidating the claimed tolerance guarantee for β<1.

Section 7 asserts that varying β solves accuracy optimization under an unfairness constraint, but does not establish the convexity or other conditions needed for that equivalence. Weighted sums generally recover only supported Pareto points. Because unfairness involves minimization over an unknown baseline, the interpretation of the resulting curves as the complete best-achievable tradeoff needs a proof or qualification.

The multiclass aggregate-only evaluation does not establish optimization tightness. Comparing an upper bound on minimum compatible unfairness with the actual classifier's unfairness concerns different quantities. Table 5 even reports an upper bound of 3.20% when actual unfairness is 0.77%. Corresponding aggregate-only lower bounds or small-instance global optima would clarify the optimization gap. Likewise, trends in the upper bounds plotted in Figure 12 do not establish trends in the underlying minima.

The practical inference claims need stronger treatment of uncertain and mismatched inputs. State-wide cancer incidence is used as the true-label rate for Bing users without establishing population comparability. Sections 6.2.2 and 7.2 also modify confusion entries or label proportions for numerical stability without propagating that modification into the reported guarantees. Mentioning interval constraints for the fair-classifier LP does not resolve these issues for the general procedures.

The measure's interpretation under imbalance is overstated. Choosing the identity confusion matrix as the baseline immediately gives unfairness ≤ error; consequently, severe disparities confined to a rare true label can have an arbitrarily small population score. This does not invalidate the definition, but it limits the claim that rare-label disparities automatically produce high unfairness. The measure describes a minimum compatible mixture fraction, rather than identifying the actual fraction of individuals subjected to unfair treatment.

The manuscript explicitly describes itself as an extension of Sabato and Yom-Tov's ICML 2020 paper, but does not clearly identify which definitions, theoretical results, algorithms, and experiments are new. A precise comparison is necessary to assess the submission's incremental originality and significance.
